rashi:a1.1: Nor the woman for her marriage contract: not in an enhancement they made. If the property was not worth the sum of the marriage contract at the time of her husband’s death and afterward it increased in value, she takes only what it was worth [then]; and not in property due as in property possessed.
rashi:a1.2: Nor the daughters: where he had undertaken to support his wife’s daughter from another man for five years; after his death she is supported only according to what the property is worth, not from the enhancement and not from property due.
rashi:a1.3: Nor the yavam: who takes a double share, his own portion and the portion of the dead brother whose wife he took in levirate marriage; he does not take [his brother’s portion] in an enhancement or in property due.
rashi:a1.4: And all of them do not take, etc.: the Gemara explains why he states it.
rashi:a2.1: Gemara. “For he is the first of his strength; the law of primogeniture is his”: this implies that it refers to him [the father]; that is, in his property there is the law of primogeniture, and not in his wife’s property.
rashi:a3.1: “Is his”: the father’s, at the time of his death.
rashi:a4.1: A creditor: who lent money to another, and the borrower sold his property and the buyers improved it; the creditor seizes the land itself and the enhancement. And this woman too is a creditor.
rashi:a4.2: Of the leniencies of a marriage contract: this is one of the leniencies of a marriage contract.
rashi:a6.1: The Merciful One calls him a firstborn: “And it shall be, the firstborn that she bears” (Deuteronomy 25:6). We establish it in Yevamot (24a) as speaking of the yavam, the Merciful One saying that the mitzva of levirate marriage falls on the eldest.
rashi:a6.2: “Shall succeed in the name of his brother”: that is, for inheritance, as is said in Yevamot (24a–b). The Merciful One calls him a firstborn, and his law is like a firstborn’s: he does not take in property due or in an enhancement between the death of their father and the levirate marriage.
rashi:a6.3: “And he has succeeded”: from the moment he married his brother’s wife, the double share is like property in his possession, and when it improved, it improved in his possession; so he takes a double share even of the enhancement.
tosafot:a4.1: In brief: Nor the woman for her marriage contract, nor the daughters for their sustenance, nor the yavam. Why does the mishna not list the husband, of whom Rav Pappa rules in Yesh Noḥalin (Bava Batra 125b) that he does not take property due as he does property possessed? Because the husband does take the enhancement: as Rabbeinu Shmuel explains there, since he is the only heir he acquires the property at once, and it improved while already his. And it seems that just as the husband does not take property due, he also does not collect his wife’s loans, even ones she made from her melog property while married to him. This is evident from Bava Kamma 42b, where he does not inherit the damages owed to his wife (according to the Rabbis) because they are like a loan; there the Gemara compares what is “due” a husband to what is “due” a firstborn, bringing the dispute of Rabbi and the Rabbis about a firstborn (Bava Batra 124a). And when Bava Batra 124b leaves the husband aside and speaks of a firstborn who does not take double in a loan, it is not because a husband does take a loan, but because the Amoraim dispute that point with regard to the firstborn. Nor may one ask why the mishna does not teach the husband together with the firstborn: for the firstborn there is an explicit mishna, as here, but that the husband does not take property due appears in no mishna or baraita, only in an Amoraic statement (Bava Batra 113a): Rabbi Abbahu said in the name of Rabbi Yannai, and some attribute it to Rabbi Yehoshua: From where do we know that the husband does not take property due as he does property possessed? As it is said: “And Seguv begot Ya’ir” [I Chronicles 2:22]. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:a4.2: In brief: Is that so? But doesn’t Shmuel say a creditor collects the enhancement? — They taught here of the leniencies of a marriage contract. Our mishna speaks of collecting from the orphans [the heirs], like the daughters’ sustenance beside it, since the sustenance of a widow and of daughters is not collected from property that was sold (Ketubot 101b). Rashi explained “the daughters” as a wife’s daughter whom the husband undertook to support; but then there would be no proof, since the case could concern an enhancement in the buyers’ hands. And the wording does not fit Rashi: why daughters rather than a son, for whom one can make the same undertaking; and why the plural, rather than “nor his wife’s daughter for her sustenance”? “Daughters” means the daughters’ sustenance owed by a stipulation of the court (Gittin 48b; Ketubot 52b). Moreover, the Gemara here gives the reason that a stipulation of the marriage contract is like the marriage contract, and a stepdaughter supported by an undertaking is not supported by a stipulation of the marriage contract but as a creditor. So the mishna means that these do not collect the enhancement from orphans, implying that a creditor does, as Shmuel said, even from orphans. Though Bava Metzia 15a says a creditor collects the enhancement from buyers because of the seller’s written guarantee, and not from one who received a gift, who has no one to turn to, an heir is different: he is “his father’s leg,” and so as not to lock the door before borrowers, the creditor collects the enhancement from him as from his father. And Bava Metzia 110a, which implies that a creditor does not collect an enhancement the orphans made, speaks of a field designated as collateral [apotiki], as does Shmuel’s rule cited there: three are paid off for their enhancement, a firstborn by an ordinary brother, a creditor by orphans and a creditor by buyers. Tosafot explains why in that case the creditor must pay for the enhancement, and why the Gemara’s first answer there (whether or not the debt equals the land and its enhancement) belongs only to the contradiction between Shmuel’s two rulings (Bava Metzia 15a; Bava Kamma 95b), not to the case of the orphans. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
gershom:a1.1: Nor the woman for her marriage contract: she does not collect her marriage contract from the enhancement by which the property improved after her husband’s death.
gershom:a2.1: Nor the daughters for their sustenance, nor the yavam. [A heading only, with no comment.]
gershom:a3.1: “And the law of primogeniture is his”: the man’s; a man must bequeath a double portion of his property to his firstborn, and not a woman.
gershom:a4.1: A creditor collects the enhancement, and the woman too is a creditor.
gershom:a5.1: They taught here of the leniencies of a marriage contract: since they were lenient with a marriage contract, in that she does not collect from medium-quality land like a creditor but from the poorest land, and likewise in that it is not collected without an oath, they were also lenient in that she does not collect the enhancement like a creditor.
gershom:a6.1: A stipulation of the marriage contract: as we learned: If he did not write for her, “Female children [you will have from me shall dwell in my house and be sustained from my property],” etc.
gershom:a7.1: The Merciful One calls him a firstborn: as we expound, “And it shall be, the firstborn”: from here we learn that the mitzva of levirate marriage falls on the eldest; “that she bears”: excluding a woman incapable of bearing children, who does not bear.
gershom:a8.1: [An editor’s note in the printed text suggests reading: “They taught only that the firstborn does not,” etc.] A firstborn does not take of the enhancement. But an enhancement that accrued between the levirate marriage and the division, [the yavam] does take.
gershom:a9.1: What is the reason? “Shall succeed in the name of his brother,” says the Merciful One, “and he has succeeded.” This is what it means: “shall succeed”: one who is yet to succeed [his brother] through levirate marriage and has not yet succeeded has the law of a firstborn, who takes of the enhancement only as an ordinary son.
gershom:a10.1: “And he has succeeded”: but once he has succeeded, having performed levirate marriage, the law of a firstborn leaves him and he stands in the place of his dead brother. He takes double in the enhancement, since between the levirate marriage and the division he takes his own portion and the portion of the dead brother; and not because of the law of the firstborn, for a firstborn has no share in an enhancement at all.
gershom:a11.1: And Rava says: even, etc. [A heading only.]
rashi:b1.1: An enhancement that comes by itself: one his brothers did not labor over.
rashi:b1.2: Such as ḥafura that became ears: the grain was green fodder at the time of his death, and now it has become ears.
rashi:b1.3: Or shalpufei that became dates: blossoms, and now they have become large dates. It teaches us that even in such an enhancement the firstborn takes only like one of the brothers: we assess what it was worth when the father died, and of that value he takes a double portion. For from the first clause I would have said that the firstborn does not take a double portion of an enhancement only where the brothers labored over it, such as manuring the fields, hoeing and digging.
rashi:b2.1: The property of the father’s father: if their grandfather was alive at the time of their father’s death, and the property was due to fall to them when he died. Even though it will certainly fall to them, and even if he had only one son, these [grandsons] take only their father’s portion. One might have thought it is like property possessed; the latter clause teaches us otherwise. For from the first clause I would have said that the “property due” of which it says the firstborn does not take refers to a case such as where the property of their father’s brother fell to them, who had sons at the time of their father’s death, and his sons died and then he died: that property was due to them at the time of their father’s death only as a possibility.
rashi:b3.1: Mishna. And one who consummates levirate marriage with his brother’s wife: and took his brother’s portion; it is a full inheritance and he does not return it in the Jubilee.
rashi:b4.1: A gift is like a sale: and goes out in the Jubilee.
rashi:b4.2: One who inherits his wife shall return: the lands to the members of her family, for payment, and he deducts for them from the payment. The Gemara explains it.
rashi:b6.1: Gemara. The inheritance of the husband is by Torah law: “To his kinsman [she’ero] who is near to him of his family, and he shall inherit it” (Numbers 27:11); from here we learn that the husband inherits his wife, in Yesh Noḥalin (Bava Batra 111b).
rashi:b7.1: “You shall return”: “each man to his possession” is a superfluous verse, for it was already said: “And you shall return each man to his possession” (Leviticus 25:10); therefore it comes to include a gift.
rashi:b8.1: And these: the other cases in the mishna; for this reason the Rabbis agree that they do not return, since they are all inheritance.
rashi:b9.1: A double portion: it juxtaposes his two portions to each other: just as his ordinary portion is an inheritance, as it is written: “On the day that he causes his sons to inherit”…
rashi:b9.2: …so too the portion of the firstborn is an inheritance. And the husband’s inheritance is by Torah law, and the yavam the Merciful One calls a firstborn.
rashi:b12.1: And they return to each other: and divide again.
rashi:b13.1: They do not return for naught: such that he would lose his firstborn share; but they do return and divide again, and he takes a double portion as at first.
rashi:b13.2: By inference, the one who says they return is saying they return for naught? Said in astonishment.
rashi:b14.1: “Wisdom is good with an inheritance”: good is the taste of the wisdom of sharp reasoning together with the inheritance of baraitot, for Rav Sheshet was a master of baraitot. Had Rav Sheshet heard this teaching of his master [presumably Rabbi Yoḥanan’s, reported by Ravin], he would not have objected at all.
rashi:b17.1: The place of his standing: for they hold seven standings [ma’amadot] for the dead.
rashi:b17.3: The value of his wife’s grave: for he is obligated to bury her, as is said in tractate Ketubot (47b).
tosafot:b1.1: To include an enhancement that comes by itself, fodder that became ears, etc.: the mishna follows the Rabbis. For Rabbi and the Rabbis disagree about whether a firstborn takes [a double portion] of an enhancement, and it concludes there [Bava Batra 124a] that they disagree about fodder that became ears and blossoms that became dates. And there too Rava says it is forbidden to act according to Rabbi’s words.
tosafot:b5.1: For a firstborn, “by giving him a double portion”: the Merciful One calls it a gift. This is puzzling: in the second chapter of Yevamot (24b) the Gemara concludes about the yavam: Rather, the Merciful One calls him a firstborn, for what halakha? To his detriment, that he does not take property due as he does property possessed. Why does it not say: to his advantage, that his firstborn share does not return in the Jubilee? One may answer: because Rabbi Elazar disagrees here and says all of them return in the Jubilee.
tosafot:b12.1: In brief: Rabbi Asi said that Rabbi Yoḥanan said: Brothers who divided are purchasers. The difficulty against Rabbi Asi from the beginning of our chapter (48a), where he said [brothers are] half heirs, and Rabbeinu Tam’s question how we can “find our hands and feet in the study hall” if we rule with Rabbi Yoḥanan that brothers who divided are purchasers and with Reish Lakish that owning the produce is not like owning the land itself, for then no one could bring first fruits except an only son of an only son back to Joshua bin Nun: I explained all of this in HaḤovel (Bava Kamma 88b) and in Beit Kor (Bava Batra 106). One may explain: even those who hold that the brothers are purchasers, since there is no retroactive clarification [bereira], did not say the shares return in the Jubilee; only Rabbi Yoḥanan said so. That is why Gittin 48a asks “how did he find his hands and feet” of Rabbi Yoḥanan in particular. All the others hold that, though the brothers are purchasers, it is only a sale that the Merciful One said returns in the Jubilee, not an inheritance or a gift, as above and as on 56b below, where it still had to be taught that brothers are purchasers and return [their shares] in the Jubilee, for we might have thought they do not. Alternatively, all division of an inheritance is learned from Joshua’s division of the land (Bava Batra 119b), and Rabbi Yoḥanan agrees that Joshua’s division does not return in the Jubilee, since it was made by prophets, by the Urim and Tummim and by scriptural decree; on this reasoning the other Amoraim disagree with him. This explains why Rav Hoshaya objects from our mishna only to Rabbi Yoḥanan, and not to the other Amoraim who hold that the brothers are purchasers and there is no bereira: only he said the shares return. And if you ask what difficulty the mishna poses for Rabbi Yoḥanan, when it is Rabbi Meir’s, and Rabbi Meir holds there is bereira in the case of one who buys wine from Cutheans (Tosefta Demai 7:4): one may answer that the Sages too do not disagree with Rabbi Meir about the firstborn, only Rabbi Elazar does. Further, even if Rabbi Meir holds bereira where a doubt is clarified by a person’s own stipulation, perhaps he does not hold it in general, as explained above (48a). Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:b14.1: Rav Ḥama read about Rav Sheshet: “Wisdom is good with an inheritance”: Rav Sheshet was a master of baraitot, as is said in HaDar (Eruvin 67a), that Rav Ḥisda’s lips would tremble at Rav Sheshet’s baraitot. And this is how the verse is read: “Wisdom is good,” the statement of Ravin in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan, “with an inheritance,” the many traditions he had, taught in baraitot.
tosafot:b17.1: The members of the family come and bury him against his will, due to a family flaw: in Nigmar HaDin (Sanhedrin 46b) we ask whether burial is because of disgrace or because of atonement; the practical difference is where one said, “Do not bury me”: if it is because of disgrace, it is not up to him. Nothing can be resolved from here, for it does not say here that he wished not to be buried at all; rather, need of money forced him to sell his grave and its path. Likewise nothing can be resolved from the case in Ketubot (48a), which says that if one said, “Do not bury me from my property,” we do not listen to him; for he does want to be buried, but means to cast himself upon the community and enrich his sons.
gershom:b1.1: To include an enhancement that comes by itself: so that you should not say that only of an enhancement the orphans made do they not take [a double share]; rather, even of an enhancement that comes by itself they do not take.
gershom:b2.1: Such as ḥafura: green fodder. That is, if the grain was fodder when he died and at the time of the division it was ears.
gershom:b3.1: Or shalpufei: he left small dates and they became large dates before the division; they do not take [a double share of the enhancement].
gershom:b4.1: To include the property of the father [our text: the father’s father]: so that you should not say that only of the property of his father’s brother does he not take a double portion, because that is due and not possessed, since his father did not know that his brother would die without offspring and had no thought at all of inheriting him; but of the property of his father’s father, which his father did have in mind to inherit, I might say that even though [the father] died before him, it is like property possessed. It teaches us that it is not.
gershom:b5.1: And these do not return in the Jubilee: even though it is written of a sale, “and it shall go out in the Jubilee, and he shall return to his possession,” the firstborn’s share and one who inherits, etc. [do not return]. The husband’s inheritance is by Torah law, as we expound: “And you shall give his inheritance to his kinsman [she’ero]”: she’ero, this is his wife.
gershom:b6.1: The Merciful One calls him a firstborn: and of the firstborn it is written “giving.”
gershom:b7.1: “You shall return, each man”: it could have said “shuvu”; from its saying “tashuvu,” [it comes] to include a gift.
gershom:b8.1: And all these cases of the mishna do not return, because they are inheritance.
gershom:b9.1: “By giving him a double portion”: of the ordinary [portion]; that is, it juxtaposes [the firstborn’s portion to the ordinary portion].
gershom:b10.1: The Merciful One calls him a firstborn, and the firstborn’s portion has already been juxtaposed to the ordinary portion.
gershom:b11.1: The husband’s inheritance is by rabbinic law: and it is not a full inheritance, and so it returns.
gershom:b12.1: They are purchasers: for we do not say there is retroactive clarification [yesh bereira], that each one inherits his own portion by Torah law; rather, there is no retroactive clarification, and they are like purchasers and return [their portions] to each other in the Jubilee. And when they return them, the firstborn’s share is not cancelled; rather, when they divide again after the Jubilee the firstborn takes his firstborn share as at first.
gershom:b13.1: Rav Sheshet objects: by inference. Since you have established “these do not return” as “they do not return for naught,” it follows that Rabbi Elazar, who disagrees and says all of them return, means they return for naught. But why should he lose his firstborn share? Rather, learn from this that this answer does not hold, and Rabbi Asi’s statement remains difficult.
gershom:b14.1: “Wisdom is good”: for he objected well. [Rabbeinu Gershom seems to read the verse as praise of Rav Sheshet’s objection.]
gershom:b15.1: And still, why did they object? Had Rav Sheshet and Rami bar Ḥama not heard what Ravin said when he came, etc.: Rabbi Elazar in the mishna means they return for naught, and the first tanna and Rabbi Meir mean they do not return for naught; so there is no difficulty for Rabbi Asi. [Rabbeinu Gershom’s text names Rami bar Ḥama where ours has Rav Ḥama, and he reads “didn’t they hear” as a question by the Gemara about both.]
gershom:b16.1: And deduct for them some of the money: of the redemption price.
gershom:b17.1: What is the purpose of the money? Why should the members of the family give him any money at all, since [on this view] he does not inherit by Torah law?
gershom:b18.1: And since he inherits by Torah law, why does he deduct for them? Because of his wife’s grave, where she is buried, for he is obligated in her burial.
gershom:b19.1: We will return to you, Yesh Bekhor LeNaḥala.
